passages.original: ac primum utrum intersit aliquid ad inferendam uel augendam miseriam post hanc uitam spiritibus hominum, si eorum corpora sepulta non fuerint, non secundum opinionem utcumque uulgatam, sed potius secundum religionis nostrae sacras litteras est uidendum. neque enim credendum est, sicut apud Maronem legitur, insepultos nauigando atque transeundo inferno amne prohiberi, quia scilicet nec ripas datur horrendas et rauca fluenta transportare prius, quam sedibus ossa quierunt. quis cor christianum inclinet his poeticis fabulosisque figmentis, cum dominus Iesus, ut inter manus inimicorum, qui eorum corpora in potestate haberent, securi occumberent christiani, nec capillum capitis eorum adserat periturum, exhortans ne timeant eos, qui cum corpus occiderint, amplius non habent quid faciant?
passages.english: And first, whether it makes any difference to the spirits of men after this life, toward bringing on or increasing their misery, if their bodies have not been buried, must be considered not according to opinion, however widely spread, but rather according to the sacred writings of our religion. For we must not believe, as is read in Maro, that the unburied are prevented from sailing and crossing the river of the underworld, because, namely, "it is not granted to carry them across the dreadful banks and hoarse streams before their bones have rested in their resting-places." Who would incline a Christian heart to these poetic and fabulous fictions, when the Lord Jesus, so that Christians might fall without anxiety into the hands of enemies who would have their bodies in their power, declares that not a hair of their head will perish, exhorting them not to fear those who, when they have killed the body, have nothing more that they can do?
passages.notes: Maro is Virgil; the quoted lines are adapted from Aeneid 6.327–328.

passages.original: Legimus in ecclesiastica historia, quam graece scripsit Eusebius et in latinam linguam uertit Rufinus, martyrum corpora in Gallia canibus exposita canumque reliquias atque ossa mortuorum usque ad extremam consumptionem ignibus concremata eosdemque cineres fluuio Rhodano, ne quid ad memoriam qualemcumque relinqueretur, inspersos.
passages.english: We read in the ecclesiastical history which Eusebius wrote in Greek and Rufinus turned into the Latin language, that the bodies of martyrs in Gaul were exposed to dogs, and that what the dogs left, and the bones of the dead, were burned with fire until they were utterly consumed, and those same ashes were scattered on the river Rhône, so that nothing of any kind should be left for a memorial.

passages.original: sed eodem ipso ferme tempore, quo id audiuimus, id est nobis apud Mediolanum constitutis Carthaginis rhetor Eulogius, qui meus in eadem arte discipulus fuit, sicut mihi ipse, posteaquam in Africam remeauimus, retulit, cum rhetoricos Ciceronis libros discipulis suis traderet, recensens lectionem, quam postridie fuerat traditurus, quendam locum offendit obscurum, quo non intellecto uix potuit dormire sollicitus. qua nocte somnianti ego illi quod non intellegebat exposui, immo non ego, sed imago mea nesciente me et tam longe trans mare aliquid aliud siue agente siue somniante et nihil de illius curis omnino curante.
passages.english: But at almost the very same time that we heard this, that is, when we were living at Milan, Eulogius, a rhetorician of Carthage, who had been my pupil in that same art, as he himself told me after we had returned to Africa, was teaching Cicero's rhetorical books to his pupils; and while going over the reading which he was to teach the next day, he came upon a certain obscure passage, and, not understanding it, he was so troubled that he could scarcely sleep. That night, as he dreamed, I explained to him what he did not understand; or rather not I, but my image, without my knowing it, while I, so far away across the sea, was either doing or dreaming something else and not caring at all about his concerns.
passages.notes: "Cicero's rhetorical books" presumably refers to De Inventione (the Rhetorici libri).
